common_name: Semmes Florida Anise (Heavy-Blooming White-Flowered Native Anise Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part to full shade; Semmes is a heavier bloomer than the wild species and stays more compact, so it fits smaller shade beds without losing floral display.

directions: Named for its origin in Semmes, Alabama, this white-flowered form of Florida anise was selected for unusually heavy spring bloom compared to typical white-flowered seedlings, covering the shrub in creamy-white, strap-petaled flowers that carry a more pungent, less sweet scent than the maroon-flowered species. It later gave rise to the cream-variegated 'Shady Lady' sport, but the parent 'Semmes' itself is grown as a solid dark-green-leaved anise valued for reliability of bloom rather than foliage variegation. Site it in consistently moist, humus-rich shade beneath high pine or hardwood canopy, where its glossy, anise-scented leaves and dense upright habit provide good year-round screening. It needs little pruning beyond removing occasional winter dieback and tolerates the Gulf South's heavy summer humidity without disease issues.
sources: JC Raulston Arboretum Plant Records

common_name: Pink Frost Illicium (Variegated Florida Anise with Cold-Induced Winter Blush)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part to full shade; give Pink Frost some winter chill exposure, since its distinctive rose-pink foliage flush is triggered by cold temperatures rather than shade or fertility.

directions: Patented as PP21287, Pink Frost is a variegated sport of Florida anise with medium-green leaves edged in cream-white, distinguishing it from both the solid dark-green species and from the differently-variegated 'Shady Lady'. Its most distinctive trait emerges in cold weather, when the cream leaf margins flush to a soft pink-rose that persists through winter before reverting to cream and green with spring warmth, and this cultivar carries deep red, many-petaled spring flowers rather than the pale pink blooms of 'Shady Lady'. It grows into a larger, more substantial shrub than most Illicium cultivars in this dataset, reaching 6 to 10 feet at maturity, so give it room in a woodland shade bed or as an informal screen. Like other Florida anise selections it tolerates wet soils and erosion-prone shaded sites and needs minimal care beyond occasional shaping.

common_name: Green Pillow Boxwood (Compact Mounding Littleleaf Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Green Pillow's naturally low, dense mound needs little to no shearing to keep its tidy shape.

directions: Green Pillow is one of the most flattened, mounding forms among littleleaf boxwood selections, staying under 18 inches tall while spreading nearly three feet wide, so it reads more as a low cushion than an upright shrub. Its bright, dense, small-leaved foliage holds good green color through winter with less bronzing than many hardy boxwood cultivars, and its naturally neat habit means it rarely needs the regular shearing that keeps most boxwood in shape. Use it for edging low borders, softening the base of taller foundation shrubs, or as a repeated accent in formal beds where a very low, unclipped mound is wanted. It is otherwise as trouble-prone as other boxwood to leafminer and blight, so give it good air circulation and avoid overhead irrigation.

common_name: Aureovariegata Boxwood (Classic Gold-Splashed Variegated English Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Aureovariegata tolerates a wider range of light than most boxwood, from full sun to fairly deep shade, without losing its variegation.

directions: One of the oldest variegated boxwood selections still in commerce, Aureovariegata carries irregular creamy-white to gold splashes and margins over dark green leaf centers, giving a mottled, painterly effect quite different from the crisp, even cream edging of 'Elegantissima' or the narrow gold picotee edge of 'Wedding Ring'. It grows larger and more loosely than most dwarf boxwood selections, slowly building into a rounded shrub several feet tall, and its slow growth rate makes it forgiving of infrequent pruning. The variegation is most pronounced on new spring growth and can fade somewhat in deep shade, so give it at least a few hours of direct or dappled sun for the best gold coloring. It works well as a light-catching accent among darker solid-green boxwood or evergreens, or sheared lightly into a small variegated hedge or topiary form.

common_name: Sienna Sunrise Nandina (Fiery Red New-Growth Heavenly Bamboo)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; new red growth flushes are most intense with several hours of direct sun and cooler temperatures.

directions: Introduced by Monrovia Nursery under patent PP14,693, Sienna Sunrise is a mid-height nandina bred around a distinctive growth pattern: each flush of new foliage emerges an intense fiery red-orange before settling to lush green for summer, then red highlights return with fall and winter cooling, giving the plant a repeating cycle of color rather than the single seasonal color change typical of most nandina. Its tight, mounding habit tops out around four feet, taller than compact selections like 'Flirt' or 'Firepower' but far more restrained than old-line cultivars such as 'Umpqua Chief'. White spring flower clusters are followed by red berries in season. It is a low-maintenance, drought-tolerant shrub once established, suited to mixed borders and foundation plantings where recurring bursts of red new growth are wanted through the growing season.

common_name: Jazz Hands Bold Loropetalum (Large-Leaf Large-Flowered Fringe Flower)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; Jazz Hands Bold grows larger and more vigorously than compact loropetalum selections, so allow a full 4-6 foot mature footprint.

directions: Patented as 'Kurenai Daiou' under US Plant Patent 27,748 and marketed as Jazz Hands Bold, this Proven Winners selection was bred for noticeably larger leaves and larger, showier fringe-like flowers than other loropetalum in its size class, distinguishing it from the smaller-flowered, smaller-leaved Jazz Hands Dwarf Pink and Jazz Hands Mini in the same breeding series. Oval leaves emerge ruby-red and mature to a purple-tinged green, setting off heavy clusters of deep pink, spidery spring flowers with lighter rebloom through the season. Its arching, spreading branch structure and 4-6 foot mature size make it suited to informal hedges, mixed shrub borders, and background plantings rather than tight foundation spaces. It shares the improved disease and pest resistance bred into the Jazz Hands series and needs only light shaping right after the main spring bloom.
sources: US Plant Patent 27,748

common_name: Jazz Hands Mini Loropetalum (Ultra-Dwarf Groundcover Fringe Flower)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; Jazz Hands Mini's very low, spreading habit suits container edges, low borders, and small-space groundcover use rather than hedging.

directions: Registered as 'Beni Hime' under US Plant Patent 27,752, Jazz Hands Mini is the smallest member of the Jazz Hands loropetalum series bred by Proven Winners, staying under 14 inches tall while spreading 3 to 4 feet wide, making it distinctly lower and flatter than the similarly-marketed but genetically separate Jazz Hands Dwarf Pink ('Kurenai'). Its dark purple foliage and hot-pink, fringe-like spring flowers match the color palette of other loropetalum, but the extreme dwarf, mat-forming habit is its defining feature, functioning more like a woody groundcover than a conventional shrub. It works well cascading over low walls, filling small foundation gaps, or edging a bed where a full-size loropetalum would quickly overwhelm the space. Light shearing after spring bloom keeps the mat dense and encourages continued flowering flushes through the season.

common_name: Daruma Loropetalum (Compact Deep Burgundy Dwarf Fringe Flower)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, loamy, slightly acidic soil (pH 4.5-6.5) in full sun to partial shade; Daruma's dwarf, dense habit needs only minimal shaping after its main spring flowering period.

directions: Daruma traces to breeding work by a Japanese nursery collaborator and was brought into US production in the early 2000s as a compact alternative to full-size loropetalum, holding at a dense 2-3 feet tall and wide without the size or vigor of cultivars like 'Miss Ruby' or 'Zhuzhou Fuchsia'. Its deep burgundy-red foliage holds its color intensely year-round rather than shifting seasonally, and in spring the plant produces profuse clusters of bright pink, fringe-like flowers that stand out sharply against the dark leaves. The tight, rounded growth habit fits foundation plantings, low hedges, and mixed borders where a small-scale but still vividly colored loropetalum is wanted. It tolerates a wide range of soils provided drainage is adequate and needs only light pruning for shape after flowering finishes.
